timeline_hubmotor_body: The project starts with a single 48V hub motor on the workbench. Does it turn, how much force does it have, and can it be controlled finely enough for a field robot? Everything that follows is built on the answer to that question.
timeline_arduino_body: Through a DAC module an Arduino drives the throttle input of the motor controller. Speed is now set by software instead of by a physical dial. This is the step from electric to controllable.
timeline_twowheels_body: Two hub motors now run together from the same Arduino. Running the left wheel faster than the right makes the robot turn, without a single moving steering part. That differential steering stays Bruut's way of turning corners for months.
timeline_rover_body: Motors, brackets and a simple frame have come together into a rolling rover. For the first time the project moves across the ground instead of across the workbench. Not a field robot yet, but proof that the drivetrain is sound.
timeline_remote_body: The rover gets a remote control so it can be steered from the sidelines. That is what makes outdoor testing practical: you can correct before something goes wrong. It is also the stepping stone to autonomy, because software can later issue those same steering commands.
timeline_firstfield_title: Into the field for the first time
timeline_firstfield_body: The first test run on real ground instead of the yard. Holes, grass and loose surfaces do something very different to a robot than a flat floor. From here on every step is tested in the field, not just thought through indoors.
timeline_rtk_body: The ArduSimple RTK receiver makes its first connection and delivers centimetre-level positioning. Ordinary GPS is metres off, which makes it useless between crop rows. This connection is the precondition for everything that later has to drive straight on its own.
timeline_codebase_title: New codebase and the first images
timeline_codebase_body: The control software moves to a new codebase in Svelte, with a browser-based operating screen. At the same time the first computer vision arrives: the robot no longer looks only at coordinates, but at what it sees. Software and camera are developed together from now on.
timeline_taskmaps_body: What the camera detects is translated into a task map of the field. That way the robot knows not only where it is, but where there is work to do. Detecting and acting come together in one system for the first time.
timeline_waypoints_body: The robot drives from waypoint to waypoint on its own, with nobody touching the transmitter. RTK position, heading and control work as a single whole here for the first time. This is the day Bruut goes from remote-controlled to autonomous.
timeline_cropmodel_title: The first model that recognises crops
timeline_cropmodel_body: A trained model recognises cauliflower plants in the row and turns them into a visualisation of where hoeing is allowed. Telling weeds and crops apart is exactly the hard part of mechanical hoeing. This is the first AI model that understands the field.
timeline_heading_title: The robot knows which way it faces
timeline_heading_body: Besides a position, the robot now has a reliable heading. Without heading you know where you are, but not which way to steer to get somewhere. With this addition, corners and lining up on a track become far calmer.
timeline_rain_title: Rained on: one step forward, two back
timeline_rain_body: A rain shower reaches the electronics and puts the robot out of action. Working outdoors means water, dust and vibration, and the build has to survive all three. The lesson from this day is baked into every enclosure and cable run that follows.
timeline_hoeing_body: Computer vision and drivetrain come together in a proof of concept: driving the row and hoeing based on what the camera sees. It is not yet an implement that lasts a full day, but it shows the idea works. From here the goal is no longer just driving, but getting work done.
timeline_tricycle_body: Steering on speed difference drags the wheels across the ground and is imprecise at low speed. So the design switches to tricycle steering, with a properly steered wheel. It drives more calmly, tracks better and suits precise work in the row far more.
timeline_purepursuitfirst_body: The robot drives a mission along AB points using the Pure Pursuit algorithm. Instead of steering at a single target, it keeps aiming at a point ahead on the line. That makes it weave less and follow the route far more smoothly.
timeline_globalshutter_body: The field robot gets a global shutter camera instead of a rolling shutter one. It captures the whole frame at once, so images taken while driving no longer skew. For detection at speed that directly improves reliability.
timeline_design_body: One long video puts every design choice for the real Bruut on the table: modular, electric, and buildable with ordinary workshop tools. Everything learned on the prototype is folded into this design. Construction of the definitive machine starts right after.
timeline_lasercut_body: The CAD drawings went to the laser cutter and came back as real sheet metal parts. That turned Bruut from a 3D model into a machine you can actually pick up. Every part is deliberately flat and simple, so anyone can have them cut locally.
timeline_wheelmodules_body: The laser-cut plates were welded together into complete wheel modules around a 48V hub motor. That module is the heart of the modular idea: the same unit fits on every corner of the robot. Want 2WD or 4WD? Simply build the same thing two or four times.
timeline_chassis_body: The tubes were drilled to size and the frame was bolted together for the first time. From this point on Bruut has a real load-bearing frame instead of a pile of loose parts. Because the joints are bolted, the frame stays adjustable later without reaching for an angle grinder.
timeline_hubmotors_body: The wheel modules with hub motors were slid under the iron frame and fixed in place. For the first time the new robot stands on its own four wheels on the ground. The drive sits inside the wheel itself, so no gearbox or chain is needed.
timeline_electronics_body: Batteries, controllers and wiring were installed and explained step by step in the video. This gave the frame its first power and a central nervous system. The layout is deliberately kept readable, so you can rebuild it and extend it yourself.
timeline_firstdrive_title: First metres on the iron frame
timeline_firstdrive_body: With the motors driven, the new machine covered its very first metres. That proved the drivetrain, power supply and controls work together in this build too. From here the focus shifted from building back to controlling.
timeline_casters_body: The rear caster wheels looked like a simple solution but turned out to be unpredictable in the field. While turning they fought back and pulled the robot off course. This failure was the deciding argument for switching to properly steered wheels.
timeline_steering_body: Two wheels each got their own stepper motor, so the steering angle can be set degree by degree. The robot's heading is now controlled purely digitally, without a mechanical steering link. This is the foundation every autonomous function relies on afterwards.
timeline_autonomous_body: With nobody touching the transmitter, the new machine also drives to a given point on its own. It picks its own heading, corrects along the way and stops at the destination. Everything learned on the prototype now works on the definitive robot.
timeline_purepursuit_body: In one uncut recording the robot completes a full Pure Pursuit mission. Nothing is edited out, so the corrections and the hesitations are visible too. No longer a few metres, but an entire route from start to finish.
timeline_precision_body: While driving AB lines the deviation stays around six centimetres on average. That order of magnitude is exactly what you need to work between crop rows later on. There is still room to improve, but the track is usable now rather than merely indicative.
timeline_speed6_body: The AB line is now followed at 6 km/h instead of walking pace. Higher speed puts sharper demands on the controller, because errors build up faster. The track staying tight anyway shows the steering has margin left for real field work.
timeline_spraybar_body: With driving under control, attention shifts to the implements behind the robot. The choice falls on a coarse-droplet spray boom instead of a misting one. Coarse droplets drift far less and suit precise driving along fixed lines.
timeline_dock_body: A concept for autonomously drilling out broad-leaved dock instead of spraying it. The plant is recognised, driven up to and dealt with mechanically, without treating the whole field. Together with the grass meter, this is the direction the implement range is heading.
timeline_grassheight_body: The robot measures grass height at points and estimates what sits between those points. That produces a picture of the whole field instead of isolated readings. It turns the field robot into a measuring instrument for grassland management as well.
